title: The hypertrophy series: the issue of intensity without volume
summary: Counterpart to his volume-without-intensity video. Low-rep, high-intensity programs struggle to grow tonnage and tend toward minimalism or excessive exercise rotation, both bad for hypertrophy. The fix is heavy strength work opening the day, followed by higher-rep work at relevant intensities.
claims: Doing very few reps is not conducive to growing tonnage; it is hard to grow tonnage with only 3 reps even if you add sets
Low-rep training traps you: a true 3RM gives minimal tonnage, while many sets of 3 you fully recover between are not truly intense since you could rep that weight more
High-intensity lifters end up with either low tonnage at high quality or high tonnage at low quality; you want both
High-intensity training tends to be minimalist, loading the same joint angles constantly and causing overuse injuries
Sticking to the big three and their variations hammers the same muscles over and over
Rotating a huge exercise selection to avoid injury means constantly relearning lifts and not reusing or fatiguing the same fibers
Powerlifters and strongmen also run hypertrophy blocks because past a point strength requires more and bigger muscle fibers
Conversely, bodybuilders need to grow their strength because it drives progressive overload
Do high intensity as strength work that opens the day, not the bulk of the program, then fill the rest with variations and accessories in higher rep ranges at relevant intensity
Offer yourself a diversity of rep ranges that represent different volumes and intensities, not ranges that all land at the same intensity
A rep range means nothing without effort: 8-12 reps can be any intensity if you do not push; he promotes leaving about a rep in the tank
